title: Ancient India, China and the Silk Roads
note: In India, Vedic religion shaped Hinduism and a ranked society, and Buddhism arose as a new path. In China, Zhou-era thinkers founded Confucianism and Daoism, the Qin unified the country in 221 BCE, and the Han opened the Silk Roads, a web of routes that carried goods and ideas across Eurasia.

read.title: Ideas on the move
text: Ancient India and China each produced ideas that still shape billions of lives. In India, the Vedas of the Indo-Aryans described gods, rituals and a society ranked into varnas, with priests at the top. Later texts developed beliefs in karma and rebirth that became central to Hinduism. Around the sixth or fifth century BCE, Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught that desire causes suffering and that a disciplined path can end it. The Maurya emperor Ashoka, shocked by the bloodshed of his own wars, embraced Buddhism and sent missionaries abroad.

In China, the breakdown of Zhou authority led to centuries of war, and thinkers asked how to restore order. Confucius stressed duty, ritual and rule by moral example. Daoists urged harmony with nature. Legalists argued for strict laws and harsh punishments. The Qin state used Legalist methods to unify China in 221 BCE, but its rule was so harsh that it fell soon after the first emperor died. The Han dynasty that followed kept the unified state and made Confucianism its official philosophy.

Han expansion into Central Asia helped connect a web of trade routes, the Silk Roads. Caravans carried silk west and brought horses, glass and silver east. Monks traveled the same routes, and Buddhism reached China this way.
